どうぞ おあがり ください — Please, come in
Make polite requests and welcome guests like a Japanese host: お～ください / ご～ください (the respectful request), ～て いただけません か (could you please…?) and ～させて いただく (allow me to…, humbly).
thank you for your effort / you must be tired
excuse me for intruding (when you enter someone's home)
to guide someone, to show them around
Could you please carry this suitcase for me?
Would you let me make the tea?
Allow me to show you the city.
To make the respectful request お + stem + ください (おかけ ください) and ご + noun + ください (ごゆっくり おすごし ください).
To ask for a favour very politely with ～て いただけません か and to know the whole ladder of requests, from ～て ください to ～て いただけない でしょう か.
To use ～させて いただく (causative + いただく) to say humbly “allow me to…” and ～させて いただけません か to ask for permission.
To know the set phrases for welcoming a Japanese guest: ようこそ, おつかれさま でした, おあがり ください, おじゃま します, ごゆっくり.

Early December, on a Saturday, at Bucharest airport. Mrs Suzuki (75) and her younger sister, Mrs Fumiko (72), are coming from Madrid: Fumiko first flew from Kyoto to Madrid, and now they are making their first trip together as sisters. They left Tama with Kenji. Mihai and Ana are waiting for them at the exit; later, at home in Cotroceni. Mihai and Ana have decided to practise the keigo they learned last week.
Oh, there they are! Mrs Suzukiii! Mrs Fumikooo!
Oh my, Ana, Mihai! Look how big the tummy has grown…
Welcome to Bucharest. It was a long journey, you must be tired.
Thank you. Mihai, excuse me, could you carry this suitcase for me? It got heavy with all the presents…
Of course. I'll take you to the car.
There's still a little snow outside. Please watch your step.
(Laughing) Ana, since when do you speak such beautiful keigo?
Last week I learned from Yuki and practised in front of a company president, Mr Tanaka.
But with us you don't need to be so formal.
We know. But just for today, would you let us practise?
(Laughing) Well, it can't be helped. Go ahead, go ahead. …Oh my, how the city sparkles!
The Christmas market has opened. Next time, allow me to show it to you at leisure.
(Arriving home) Please, come in. Please use these slippers.
Excuse me for intruding. Oh my, what high ceilings!
Please have a seat here. I'll make some tea now, please wait a moment.
Oh, Ana, wait. The tea — would you let me make it? I brought tea from Kyoto.
But to have you, our guests, do something like…
It's fine, dear. Whoever has a big tummy sits down. Today I'll have the pleasure of making the tea.
Fumiko's tea is the best in the world. Even though I couldn't drink it for fifty years.
Then we'll gladly accept. …Mrs Suzuki, how is Tama?
Fine. Kenji sends me photos every day. She has truly become the ramen shop's cat.
(Laughing) Both of you, please, relax and take your time with us.

i-ta-da-ke-ma-sen-ka: seven even syllables, and at the end your voice rises slightly on “ka”. Don't swallow “ke”: i-ta-da-ke, not “itadaks”.
sa-se-te i-ta-da-ki-mas: a short “se” with a clean “s” (not “sh”). At the end, “mas” with an almost silent “u”.
yoo-ko-so: a long “yō”, as long as two syllables. o-ja-ma: “ja” as in “jam”, not “ya”. Say them with a smile and a small bow.
1. お～ください / ご～ください: the respectful request

In chapter 36 you learned お～に なる (respect for what the other person does). If you want to ASK the other person to do something, drop に なる and add ください: お + stem (～ます without ます) + ください. It's more polite than ～て ください, and you hear it everywhere in Japan: in shops, stations, hotels, at Mrs Fumiko's teahouse.
あがる (to step into the house)

With Sino-Japanese verbs with する, put ご in front of the noun and drop する: れんらく する → ごれんらく ください (please contact us), りよう する → ごりよう ください (please use), ちゅうい する → ごちゅうい ください (please be careful!). And ごゆっくり (at leisure) often goes in front: ごゆっくり おすごし ください.

As with お～する, don't use お～ください with verbs whose stem is one syllable: ✗ おみ ください, ✗ おね ください. For them there are special words (ごらん ください). And don't confuse it with the humble form: おまち します = I will wait for you; おまち ください = YOU please wait.

In English, “Come in!” and “Have a seat!” are imperatives too, softened by tone or by “please”. Japanese softens the imperative through the verb form itself: お～ください is an imperative “wearing white gloves”. When you hear あしもと に おきをつけ ください on the underground, that's exactly it: “mind your step”, said with respect.
2. ～て いただけません か: “could you please…?”

When you ask for a favour, Japanese doesn't give orders; it ASKS whether you might receive the favour. いただく (the humble form of もらう, ch. 37) → potential form いただける (to be able to receive) → negative + か: いただけません か = “couldn't I receive (the favour of you doing…)?” The person doing the action is the other person; you mark them with に: ミハイさん に もって いただく.

The negative makes the request softer, just like in English: “Wouldn't you mind…?”, “Couldn't you…?” sound more polite than “Can you…?”. The positive form いただけます か exists too and is only slightly less delicate. You often start with すみません が, … or もうしわけ ありません が, … (“excuse me, but…”).
Excuse me, could you carry this suitcase for me?
Could you give me the phone number? (Fumiko, ch. 18)
I wonder if you could possibly speak a little more slowly.
The usual answer: はい、いい です よ / もちろん です (of course). If you can't: すみません、ちょっと…. Japanese people rarely say a direct “no”; “ちょっと…” with a pause is already a polite refusal.
3. ～させて いただく: “allow me to…”

Here two things you already know meet: the causative ～させる (ch. 33, to let someone do) and いただく (to receive, humble). ～させて いただく = “I (humbly) receive permission to do” → “allow me to…”, “with your permission, …”. The action is YOURS, but you present it as a gift received from the other person.
I'll take the day off (with your permission)

If you are only ASKING for permission, use the request form from section 2: ～させて いただけません か = “would you allow me to…?”. Simpler and still polite: ～させて ください. Mihai: きょう だけ は れんしゅう させて いただけません か (would you let us practise, just for today?). Fumiko: おちゃ を いれさせて いただけません か.
We are closed today. (notice on a shop door)
Are you really letting us use this room?

A mistake even Japanese people make: an extra “さ” with godan verbs. ✗ いかさせて いただきます, ✗ よまさせて いただきます. Correct: いかせて, よませて (the godan causative is ～あせる, without さ). And don't overdo it: if you put させて いただく in every sentence, it sounds stiff.
4. How to welcome a Japanese guest (and how to enter someone's home)
Welcoming a guest in Japanese follows a real “script”, with set lines. Ana and Mihai followed it almost exactly. Here are the lines, in the order they are said.

おじゃま します literally means “I'm disturbing you” (じゃま = disturbance). You say it when you enter someone's home or an office; when leaving you say it in the past: おじゃま しました. あがる (“to go up”) comes from Japanese houses, where the floor is higher than the entrance (げんかん): you take off your shoes and “step up” into the house. That's why Ana has スリッパ ready.

Just as a host anywhere insists “have another piece!”, in Japan too the guest first politely declines and the host insists. When Fumiko says “きょう は わたし が いれさせて いただきます”, it's an elegant kind of insisting: although she is a guest, she asks “permission” to serve.
5. Three ways of asking, in short
The three constructions of this chapter differ in who does the action and how directly you ask.
respectful request, almost a set phrase
question: will you do me the favour?

お～ください is used when it's clear the other person will do the thing (sit down, come in): it's an invitation. ～て いただけません か is for real favours that cost the other person something (carrying your suitcase). Review from ch. 36–37: めしあがって ください (respect), いただきます (humble), おまち します (humble, I) versus おまち ください (respect, you).

Keigo creates distance. Between close friends or in the family, too much keigo sounds like a joke or like coldness. That's why Mrs Fumiko says “わたし たち に は、そんな に かたく ならなくて も いい の よ”. Mihai and Ana do it only today, as practice, and everyone laughs.

ドア の かみ — The note on the door
The sisters are sleeping in the baby's room, which is still almost empty. On the door, Ana has stuck a note written in Japanese, with respectful request phrases.
This room belongs to the baby who will be born in January. Until then, please use it, both of you.

ごじゅうねん おくれ の りょこう — A trip fifty years late
On the evening before Mrs Suzuki and Mrs Fumiko arrived, Mihai and Ana tidied up the baby's room.
The room was still almost empty. The baby's cot was also still in its box.
“The grannies get to sleep here before the baby does,” Ana said with a laugh, as she spread the futons on the floor.
Their neighbour, Mrs Doina, lent them two thick blankets. “It would be a shame if our guests from Japan caught a cold.”
Ana asked Mrs Doina: “Next week we're having a Japanese tea gathering at our place. We'd be so happy if you came. Could you?”
“Of course! I'll bring the other neighbours too.”
Then Ana wrote a few polite words in Japanese on a little piece of paper and stuck it on the door of the room.
After that, the two of them practised keigo in front of the mirror.
“Please, come in.” “Please have a seat here.” Every time Ana said something, Mihai played the guest and bowed deeply.
When they swapped roles, Mihai said cheerfully at the entrance: “Excuse me for intruding!”
“Mihai, that's the guest's line!” Ana held her tummy with laughter.
On Saturday at noon, the airport exit was full of people. Mihai was holding a sheet of paper on which he had written “Welcome” in big letters.
After a while, two tiny old ladies came out, holding hands.
They were both wearing scarves of the same colour. They were matching scarves that Mrs Fumiko had bought in Kyoto.
When Ana waved to them, Mrs Suzuki was about to break into a run like a child. Mrs Fumiko quickly tugged at her sleeve: “Sister, careful!”
Mrs Suzuki gently placed her hand on Ana's tummy. “Hello. It's your grandma from Madrid.”
Just then, the baby gave a little kick inside. Tears welled up in Mrs Suzuki's eyes.
“Come on, let's take a photo all together,” said Mrs Fumiko.
And she politely asked a young man who was nearby, in Japanese: “Excuse me, could you take a photo of us?”
The young man looked puzzled, but when he saw the camera and Mrs Fumiko's smile, he seemed to understand straight away.
“Even if you don't understand the language, the heart of a request still gets through,” said Mrs Fumiko.
In the photo, all four were holding the “Welcome” sheet and laughing.
In the car, Mrs Fumiko kept looking out of the window. “It's truly the first time my sister and I have travelled, just the two of us.”
When they were young, the two of them had promised to go to Hokkaido, all three of them, with their mother. But before that, Mrs Suzuki had left for Spain.
“It's a trip fifty years late,” said Mrs Suzuki, and Mrs Fumiko laughed: “Then let's enjoy it twice as much, for all the time we're late.”
Mihai, at the wheel, watched them in the rear-view mirror and felt his heart grow warm.
After a while, a big gate came into view through the window.
“Oh, it looks like Paris!” said Mrs Suzuki, and Mihai explained:
“It's the Arc de Triomphe. Bucharest used to be called ‘Little Paris’.”
Mrs Suzuki said, “It looks a little like Madrid too,” and gently squeezed Mrs Fumiko's hand.
When they got home, Mrs Fumiko opened the suitcase and took out the presents one after another.
Tea and yatsuhashi from Kyoto, Spanish turrón from Mrs Suzuki and, on top of that, a ramen soup base that Kenji had entrusted to them.
“Kenji said: ‘Whenever Ana feels like having some, make Mihai cook it.’”
Mihai scratched his head. “If I make it, Kenji will scold me.”
Ana laughed and put the box of turrón on the shelf.
After reading the note on the baby's room door, Mrs Fumiko was silent for a while.
“Are you really letting us use this room? It's the baby's precious room, isn't it?”
“The baby is still in my tummy. We want the two of you to be the first to use it.”
In the evening, Mihai's mother, Elena, came with sarmale. It was the first time they had seen each other since the wedding.
Elena and the sisters have no language in common. But Mihai translated, and soon the table was full of laughter.
After the meal, Mrs Fumiko made Kyoto tea again.
Elena, drinking green tea for the first time, made a face: “Bitter!” But at the second sip she said: “Oh, it's good.”
Mrs Fumiko said happily: “Please do come to next week's tea gathering as well.”
Then Mrs Suzuki spoke to Mihai, a little solemnly:
“Mihai, I have a favour to ask. Your grandfather in the mountain village that Ana told us about… could you possibly take us to meet him?”
Mihai was a little surprised, then smiled. “Of course. Next week, allow me to take you to the village.”
“Grandpa will be so happy. He's never had guests from Japan,” Ana added.
Late that night, when Ana got up to drink some water, she heard soft laughter coming from the baby's room.
“I wish we could have shown this to Mother too.” “I'm sure she's watching from somewhere.”
Just like when they were little girls, the two of them kept whispering and giggling, and whispering again.
Ana smiled quietly in front of the door and went back to bed.
“Mihai, I'm so glad that the first guests in that room are those two.”
Mihai answered in an already sleepy voice: “Yes. She's happy about it too, I'm sure.” Inside the tummy came another little kick.
